name: CRR_CTChest_Adult_Indicators
title: CT Chest - Adult: referral indicators
publisher: Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora - Community Referred Radiology Programme
description: Atomic clinical indicators for the CT Chest (Adult) national referral criteria (National Community Referral Criteria for Imaging Part I, v2.0, published 09/04/2026, pp.12-16). Evaluated by the CQL library CRR_CTChest_Adult. Each answer may carry the answer-evidence extension (status documented|inferred, quote). NOT CLINICALLY REVIEWED. No item carries an initialExpression: no population library exists for this site.

item.text: Patient
Age in years at referral
Current smoker
Symptoms and signs
Haemoptysis occurred in the absence of chest infection
Unexplained, new, or worsening dyspnoea
Unexplained cough, persisting and worsening for more than 3 weeks
Unexplained chest and/or shoulder pain persisting for more than 3 weeks
Unexplained changes in existing symptoms in patients with underlying chronic respiratory problems persisting for more than 3 weeks
Unexplained hoarseness persisting for more than 3 weeks
Repeated / or unresolved chest infections
Persistent, unexplained haemoptysis
Unexplained weight loss and loss of appetite persisting for more than 3 weeks
Un-investigated/unexplained abnormal chest signs persisting for more than 3 weeks. (e.g. suspected pleural effusion)
New, supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
Features suggestive of paraneoplastic syndromes. e.g. hypercalcaemia, hypertrophic osteoarthropathy with finger (and toe) clubbing and painful swollen joints
New cervical lymphadenopathy persisting for more than 3 weeks and nodes are more than 1 cm in diameter in a patient with other lung cancer symptoms or signs or risk factors
The concerning symptoms or signs are of new onset
Symptoms or signs persistent for six weeks despite appropriate treatment
Persistent, non-specific, non-localising symptoms and signs which are concerning for underlying cancer
Haemoptysis
Haemoptysis
Initial assessment and investigations
Upper respiratory tract causes, including bleeding from the nasopharynx, sinuses or oral cavity, have been excluded
Chest X-ray completed as part of initial investigations
Blood tests completed as part of initial investigations
Initial investigations fail to identify a cause
Chest x-ray is normal
Indeterminate abnormality on chest x-ray which raises the possibility of a lung cancer (e.g. bulky hilum)
Persistent consolidation on chest x-ray done as a 6-week follow-up study
Isolated pulmonary nodule identified on a chest x-ray
The nodule cannot be confirmed as benign from x-ray appearances alone
The radiology report recommends the requested imaging
Patient re-presents with the symptoms or signs being referred (this is not the initial presentation)
The request is for follow-up of a nodule discovered incidentally on a CT chest scan
The radiology report confirms the nodule is benign based on CT appearance and no follow-up is required
Specialist, PCRL or radiologist advice
A secondary care clinician or radiologist advises referral for urgent staging CT chest/liver for work up of a suspicious lesion on chest x-ray
CT is the advised next step on the local HealthPathway, as opposed to referral to secondary care or PET-CT
A secondary care clinician, Primary Care Radiology Liaison (PCRL) or radiologist advises referral for urgent imaging of the requested exam
A secondary care clinician, Primary Care Radiology Liaison (PCRL) or radiologist advises referral for a non-urgent scan
Name and role of the clinician who advised (must be included in the referral)
